qualification: NSSCO Economics 6145 (syllabus vNIED 2018; implementation 2019; first examination 2020, examined 2026)

items.prompt: Identify two groups with conflicting interests where a profitable workshop’s waste damages neighbouring gardens.
items.canonical_answer: Workshop owners gain private profit while neighbouring residents bear external damage.
marking_guidance: Feature/example (1): owners’ private gain. Distinct characteristic/example (1): neighbours’ external cost.
objective_titles: Discuss conflicts of interest in relation to: - social costs* and benefits, private costs and benefits - short/long term costs and benefits - conserving resources versus exploiting resources - free trade versus protection - public expenditure versus private expenditure

items.prompt: Explain the error in equating any reed harvesting with unsustainable overexploitation when regeneration can support a monitored lower harvest.
items.canonical_answer: Harvesting is resource exploitation or use. It becomes overexploitation when use exceeds sustainable limits or causes the relevant unsustainable damage; the lower managed option must be assessed from those conditions.
marking_guidance: Confusion (1): use equated with overuse. Boundary/test (1): regeneration and damage conditions distinguish them.
objective_titles: Discuss conflicts of interest in relation to: - social costs* and benefits, private costs and benefits - short/long term costs and benefits - conserving resources versus exploiting resources - free trade versus protection - public expenditure versus private expenditure

items.prompt: Explain the error in reporting only N$5,000 external damage as social cost when the same activity also has N$8,000 private cost.
items.canonical_answer: Social cost is private plus external cost: N$13,000. External damage is the third-party component, not the whole social cost.
marking_guidance: Confusion (1): component mistaken for whole. Boundary/test (1): N$8,000 + N$5,000 = N$13,000.
objective_titles: Discuss conflicts of interest in relation to: - social costs* and benefits, private costs and benefits - short/long term costs and benefits - conserving resources versus exploiting resources - free trade versus protection - public expenditure versus private expenditure

items.prompt: Evaluate two feasible methods with private benefit N$12,000 each and no external benefits: original private cost N$8,000/external cost N$5,000; cleaner private cost N$9,000/external cost N$1,000.
items.canonical_answer: Original private net benefit N$4,000 exceeds cleaner N$3,000, but original social net benefit −N$1,000 is below cleaner N$2,000. The cleaner method is supported on the stated social basis, conditional on full comparable effects and feasibility; who bears its cost still matters.
marking_guidance: Argument for (2): relevant gain (1), developed consequence or numerical evidence (1). Argument against (2): opposing cost/interest (1), developed consequence (1). Condition (1): decisive feasibility, time or management requirement. Judgement (2): conditional choice (1), linked to the actual comparison (1). Total 7.
objective_titles: Discuss and evaluate social and private costs and benefits with opposing effects, a decisive condition and a justified conclusion.

items.prompt: Evaluate a larger current reed harvest that raises this season’s earnings but is documented to damage regeneration and reduce future work; a lower managed harvest is feasible.
items.canonical_answer: Current earnings support the larger harvest, but regeneration damage threatens future livelihoods and services. Prefer a managed level if it preserves future functions and allows feasible current livelihoods; the short-term gain alone is insufficient.
marking_guidance: Argument for (2): relevant gain (1), developed consequence or numerical evidence (1). Argument against (2): opposing cost/interest (1), developed consequence (1). Condition (1): decisive feasibility, time or management requirement. Judgement (2): conditional choice (1), linked to the actual comparison (1). Total 7.
objective_titles: Discuss and evaluate short-term and long-term costs and benefits with opposing effects, a decisive condition and a justified conclusion.

items.prompt: Evaluate a proposed ban against a monitored lower reed harvest where regeneration supports the lower level and households rely on some harvest income.
items.canonical_answer: A ban conserves more of the resource but removes current livelihood output. Managed use can retain income and regeneration under the stated conditions. Prefer credible sustainable management if monitoring works; choose stricter conservation if damage persists.
marking_guidance: Argument for (2): relevant gain (1), developed consequence or numerical evidence (1). Argument against (2): opposing cost/interest (1), developed consequence (1). Condition (1): decisive feasibility, time or management requirement. Judgement (2): conditional choice (1), linked to the actual comparison (1). Total 7.
objective_titles: Discuss and evaluate conservation and exploitation of resources with opposing effects, a decisive condition and a justified conclusion.

items.prompt: Evaluate a temporary basket tariff with credible efficiency training and a review date, where local producers gain room to adjust but buyers face higher prices.
items.canonical_answer: Protection can support producers and adjustment during training, but higher buyer costs and weaker competition are limitations. Conditional time-limited support is defensible if improvement is feasible and review removes ineffective protection; permanent support is not established.
marking_guidance: Argument for (2): relevant gain (1), developed consequence or numerical evidence (1). Argument against (2): opposing cost/interest (1), developed consequence (1). Condition (1): decisive feasibility, time or management requirement. Judgement (2): conditional choice (1), linked to the actual comparison (1). Total 7.
objective_titles: Discuss and evaluate free trade and protection with opposing effects, a decisive condition and a justified conclusion.

items.prompt: Evaluate tax-funded public access-path spending where several producers will use it regularly, maintenance is funded, but taxes reduce private purchases and another useful project is forgone.
items.canonical_answer: Shared access and lower delivery barriers support the path. Tax withdrawal and the displaced project are opportunity costs. Support requires the path’s useful shared gains to exceed the feasible alternatives, with distribution and maintenance considered; public ownership alone does not decide.
marking_guidance: Argument for (2): relevant gain (1), developed consequence or numerical evidence (1). Argument against (2): opposing cost/interest (1), developed consequence (1). Condition (1): decisive feasibility, time or management requirement. Judgement (2): conditional choice (1), linked to the actual comparison (1). Total 7.
objective_titles: Discuss and evaluate public and private expenditure with opposing effects, a decisive condition and a justified conclusion.

items.prompt: Identify private and external costs where a workshop pays wages and its dust damages neighbours’ gardens (2). Identify short- and long-term effects where intensive harvest raises current earnings but damages future regeneration (2). Explain the conservation conflict for households relying on harvest income (2). Identify expenditure types for a government-funded shared path and a household’s own basket purchase (2).
items.canonical_answer: Wages are private cost; garden damage external cost. Current earnings are short-term and later regeneration damage long-term. Conservation preserves future resources but can reduce current livelihood output. The path is public spending and the household purchase private spending.
marking_guidance: Identification, separate points (2): wages private (1), gardens external (1). Time effects (2): current earnings (1), future damage (1). Explanation (2): future resource benefit (1), current income sacrifice (1). Spending (2): public path (1), private purchase (1). Marks allocation 8.

items.prompt: Invented Reedplain workshop: private benefit N$12,000, private cost N$8,000, external garden damage N$5,000 for one period, no external benefit. Intensive harvest raises current earnings but damages future regeneration; a lower monitored harvest can preserve regeneration and some livelihoods. A proposed basket tariff supports producers but raises buyer prices; training and review are feasible. A tax-funded shared path improves regular delivery access, while reducing private purchasing power and displacing another useful public project; maintenance is funded. Describe three private/social/time features with case details (6). Explain the social-cost calculation and the conflict between current and future effects (7). Discuss managed harvest, protection and path spending together, weighing the affected interests (7).
items.canonical_answer: Private cost is N$8,000, external damage N$5,000 and current earnings contrast with future regeneration loss. Social cost N$13,000 exceeds benefit N$12,000, so private net gain N$4,000 coexists with social net loss N$1,000. Intensive use supports present income but weakens future resources. Managed harvest can retain livelihoods; temporary protection needs credible improvement because buyers pay; the path needs gains exceeding forgone alternatives. Conditional targeted measures are stronger than unrestricted support.
marking_guidance: Data description (6): private expense (1), N$8,000 detail (1); external damage (1), N$5,000 detail (1); time conflict (1), current income/future regeneration detail (1). Mechanism/explanation (7): social cost sum (1), N$13,000 (1), social net −N$1,000 (1), private gain N$4,000 (1); external omission changes judgement (1), current income benefit (1), later resource loss (1). Both sides/judgement (7): managed livelihood benefit (1), conservation/monitoring constraint (1); protection adjustment benefit (1), buyer-cost/review limitation (1); path shared benefit versus private/other-project opportunity cost (1); condition credible sustainable affordable implementation (1); judgement targeted conditional support linked to all three choices (1). Marks allocation 6+7+7=20.

items.prompt: Invented resource communities. Case 1: current harvesting provides private jobs/income; a monitored level preserves regeneration. A temporary tariff has credible efficiency training/review but raises consumer prices. A regularly used public access path has funded maintenance but requires taxes that reduce private spending. Case 2: extraction causes irreversible long-term resource damage; producer protection lacks an improvement plan while imposing high costs on buyers; a proposed public path is rarely used and would displace valuable water provision. Free trade offers cheaper goods in both cases but exposes current producers to adjustment. Evaluate managed use, temporary protection and public-path spending in Case 1 (7). Evaluate the proposed package in Case 2, including conservation, trade interests and the alternative use of public funds (7).
items.canonical_answer: Case 1: sustainable harvesting retains income, temporary protection may support credible adjustment and a useful path can serve several users. Consumer and taxpayer costs remain. Conditional support requires monitoring, review and gains exceeding private alternatives. Case 2: irreversible damage favours conservation; costly protection without improvement weakens the case against cheaper trade with adjustment support. Rarely used path spending is poorly supported where valuable water provision is displaced. Reject the package as described, conditional on those facts rather than a blanket opposition to resource use or public spending.
marking_guidance: Case 1 marks (7): argument for livelihood/sustainable use (1), credible producer adjustment (1), useful public access (1); opposing resource risk if monitoring fails (1), consumer/taxpayer opportunity costs (1); condition effective monitoring/review and net value (1); judgement conditional package support linked to three choices (1). Case 2 allocation (7): argument for current producer income/jobs (1), possible shared-access aim (1); argument against irreversible resource loss (1), costly ineffective protection (1), displaced water provision (1); condition supplied long-term damage and weak plans (1); judgement reject package with conservation/open-trade adjustment/valuable-spending alternative (1). Total 14.
